content.title: About
content.content: Gluten‑free bread is a baked product made from gluten‑free ingredients such as rice, corn, buckwheat or tapioca flour. It is intended for people with celiac disease, gluten sensitivity, or those who choose a gluten‑free diet. Flavor and texture can differ from traditional wheat bread, but modern formulations achieve a soft crust and airy crumb.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first gluten‑free breads appeared in the 1970s in the United States as a response to the rising number of celiac patients.
Gluten‑free blends often contain xanthan gum or guar gum to mimic the elasticity of gluten.
There are more than 30 types of gluten‑free flours, each giving the bread its own distinct taste and color.
Some gluten‑free breads are fortified with probiotics and prebiotics to support gut microbiota.
In Russia, gluten‑free bread became popular in the 2010s and is now available in most major supermarkets.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Gluten‑free bread contains no gluten, which can trigger intestinal inflammation in people with celiac disease.

items.title: Lower glycemic index
items.content: Bread made from whole‑grain gluten‑free flours (e.g., buckwheat) typically has a lower glycemic index than regular wheat bread.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Many recipes include psyllium, flax seeds or whole grains, boosting dietary fiber content.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fortified versions may contain iron, vitamin B12 and folate, nutrients often lacking in a gluten‑free diet.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: Complex carbohydrates in gluten‑free bread provide steady energy without sharp blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Some gluten‑free breads contain high amounts of sugar, salt or fats to improve taste.

items.title: Allergy to other ingredients
items.content: Recipes may include nuts, soy or dairy, which can cause allergic reactions.

items.title: Lower protein levels
items.content: Gluten‑free bread often has less protein than wheat bread, so it should be paired with other protein sources.

items.title: Shelf‑life
items.content: Without gluten, the crumb structure can be less stable, causing the bread to stale more quickly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Gluten‑free bread works well for sandwiches, toast, serving alongside soups and salads. It can be toasted, used for breading, or made into croutons. When stored in the refrigerator it stays softer longer than at room temperature.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep gluten‑free bread in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, freeze it, preferably sliced into portions. Before use, allow it to thaw at room temperature or warm it in a toaster.
